terms.definition: Money is what we use to buy things.
terms.analogy: Money is like a token you swap for things you want.
terms.example: You give $2 and get an apple.

terms.definition: A price is how much money a thing costs.
terms.analogy: A price is like a tag on a toy.
terms.example: The toy has a price of $5.

terms.definition: A company is a group of people who make or sell things.
terms.analogy: A company is like a team. Each person has a job.
terms.example: A shop that bakes bread is a company.

terms.definition: A product is a thing that a company sells.
terms.analogy: A product is what sits on the shelf in a shop.
terms.example: A loaf of bread is a product.

terms.definition: A customer is a person who buys from a company.
terms.analogy: A customer is the one who walks into the shop.
terms.example: Mia is a customer. She buys a loaf of bread.

terms.definition: An owner is a person who owns a part of a company.
terms.analogy: You own your bike. An owner owns a part of a company.
terms.example: Sam owns half of the shop, so Sam is an owner.

terms.definition: A stock is a small piece of a company that you can own.
terms.analogy: A stock is like one slice of a big pie.
terms.example: You own a stock of a shop. You own a bit of the shop.

terms.definition: A share is one unit of a stock.
terms.analogy: A share is like one slice of the pie.
terms.example: You buy 3 shares. Now you own 3 slices.

terms.definition: A market is a place where people buy and sell.
terms.analogy: A market is like a fair with many stalls.
terms.example: A farm market sells fruit, eggs and bread.

terms.definition: The stock market is a place where people buy and sell stocks.
terms.analogy: The stock market is like a big fair for pieces of companies.
terms.example: On the stock market, Mia buys 2 shares of a toy company.

terms.definition: An exchange is a business that runs a stock market.
terms.analogy: An exchange is like the mall that holds many shops.
terms.example: The NYSE and the Nasdaq are two big exchanges.

terms.definition: The NYSE is the New York Stock Exchange, a big US exchange.
terms.analogy: The NYSE is like a big old mall.
terms.example: A famous shoe company can list its stock on the NYSE.

terms.definition: The Nasdaq is a big US exchange. Many tech companies are there.
terms.analogy: The Nasdaq is like a mall full of tech shops.
terms.example: A phone company can list its stock on the Nasdaq.

terms.definition: Profit is the money you make when you sell for more than you paid.
terms.analogy: You buy a toy for $5 and sell it for $8. You keep $3.
terms.example: Buy at $10, sell at $12. Your profit is $2.

terms.definition: A loss is money you lose when you sell for less than you paid.
terms.analogy: You buy a toy for $5 and sell it for $3. You lose $2.
terms.example: Buy at $10, sell at $7. Your loss is $3.

terms.definition: A trade is one buy or one sell of a stock.
terms.analogy: A trade is like a swap. Money for stock, or stock for money.
terms.example: Mia buys 2 shares today. That is one trade.

terms.definition: A trader is a person who buys and sells stocks.
terms.analogy: A trader is like a shopper who buys and sells all day.
terms.example: Sam is a trader. He makes many trades.

terms.definition: A ticker is a short code for a stock, like AAPL.
terms.analogy: A ticker is like a nickname for a stock.
terms.example: AAPL is the ticker for Apple.

terms.definition: An ETF is a box that holds stocks.
terms.analogy: An ETF is like a bag of mixed fruit.
terms.example: SPY is an ETF. One share gives you a bit of 500 companies.

terms.definition: An ADR lets you buy a foreign stock in the US.
terms.analogy: An ADR is a bridge that brings a foreign stock here.
terms.example: TSM is an ADR. It is a Taiwan company you can buy in the US.

terms.definition: A suffix is the tag at the end of a ticker. It shows where a stock trades.
terms.analogy: A suffix is like a zip code on a letter.
terms.example: In AAPL.L, the .L says it trades in London.

terms.definition: An IPO is when a company first sells its stock to people.
terms.analogy: An IPO is like a big first day for a stock.
terms.example: The toy company had its IPO in May.

terms.definition: A CEO is the boss of a company.
terms.analogy: A CEO is like the captain of a ship.
terms.example: Mia is the CEO of a toy company.

terms.definition: EPS is the profit a company made for each share.
terms.analogy: EPS is the slice of profit that each share gets.
terms.example: A company made $100 and has 50 shares. EPS is $2.

terms.definition: P/E is the price you pay for $1 of profit.
terms.analogy: P/E is the price tag on each dollar of profit.
terms.example: A stock with a P/E of 10 costs $10 for each $1 of profit.

terms.definition: GDP shows how much a country makes in a year.
terms.analogy: GDP is the score for a whole country.
terms.example: When GDP goes up, a country grows.

terms.definition: The Fed is the bank of the US. It helps set the cost of loans.
terms.analogy: The Fed is like a boss for money in the US.
terms.example: When the Fed acts, many stock prices can move.

terms.definition: The FOMC is a team in the Fed that votes on loan costs.
terms.analogy: The FOMC is like a team that votes on a rule.
terms.example: The FOMC meets 8 times a year.

terms.definition: CPI shows how fast prices are rising.
terms.analogy: CPI is like a gauge for prices.
terms.example: If CPI is up, things cost more than last year.

terms.definition: ATH is the highest price a stock has hit.
terms.analogy: ATH is like a new world record.
terms.example: The stock hit an ATH of $50 today.

terms.definition: ATL is the lowest price a stock has hit.
terms.analogy: ATL is like the bottom of the stairs.
terms.example: The stock hit an ATL of $2 today.

terms.definition: EOD means the end of the day.
terms.analogy: EOD is like the last bell at school.
terms.example: The EOD price is the last price of the day.

terms.definition: After-hours is the time after the stock market closes for the day.
terms.analogy: After-hours is like a shop that stays open late.
terms.example: The news came out in AH, so the price moved.

terms.definition: Pre-market is the time before trading starts.
terms.analogy: Pre-market is like a warm-up before a game.
terms.example: At 8 AM, pre-market prices show the first moves.

terms.definition: OTC stocks trade away from the big exchanges.
terms.analogy: OTC is like a yard sale, not a big store.
terms.example: A tiny company may trade OTC, not on an exchange.

terms.definition: DD means you read up on a stock first.
terms.analogy: DD is like trying a toy first.
terms.example: Before I buy, I do DD on the company.

terms.definition: HODL means you keep a stock and do not sell.
terms.analogy: HODL is like keeping a seed in the ground.
terms.example: She will HODL her shares for five years.

terms.definition: FOMO is the fear of missing out.
terms.analogy: FOMO is when you see friends play and want in.
terms.example: The stock jumped, and FOMO made me want to buy.

terms.definition: YOLO is when you bet lots of money on one stock.
terms.analogy: YOLO is like a big bet on one game.
terms.example: A YOLO trade can win big, but it can lose big too.

terms.definition: The bid is the top price a buyer will pay right now.
terms.analogy: The bid is what a buyer will pay.
terms.example: The bid is $10. A buyer will pay $10.

terms.definition: The ask is the low price a seller wants right now.
terms.analogy: The ask is what a seller wants.
terms.example: The ask is $10.05. A seller wants $10.05.

terms.definition: Volume is how many shares were bought and sold.
terms.analogy: Volume is like how busy a store is.
terms.example: A stock with high volume has many trades.

terms.definition: Market cap is the price of one share times all the shares.
terms.analogy: Market cap is like the price tag on a whole company.
terms.example: A stock costs $10 and has 1,000 shares. Its market cap is $10,000.

terms.definition: RSI is a number from 0 to 100. It shows how fast a price moved.
terms.analogy: RSI is like a speed gauge for a price.
terms.example: A high RSI means a price rose fast.

terms.definition: MACD shows if a price move is gaining speed.
terms.analogy: MACD is like a gas pedal in a car.
terms.example: The MACD can show a price is losing speed.

terms.definition: VWAP is the middle price of the day. Busy times count more.
terms.analogy: VWAP is like a line that hugs the crowd.
terms.example: Price over VWAP is high for the day.

terms.definition: A bull is a person who thinks prices will rise.
terms.analogy: A bull swings its horns up.
terms.example: In a bull market, prices rise for a long time.

terms.definition: A bear is a person who thinks prices will fall.
terms.analogy: A bear swipes its paw down.
terms.example: In a bear market, prices fall for a long time.

terms.definition: An index is a list of stocks that shows how a group is doing.
terms.analogy: An index is like a class score made from many kids.
terms.example: An index of 500 big companies shows how they all do.

terms.definition: The S&P 500 is an index of 500 big US companies.
terms.analogy: The S&P 500 is like a team photo of big US companies.
terms.example: If the S&P 500 is up, many big stocks rose that day.

terms.definition: The Dow is an index of 30 big US companies.
terms.analogy: The Dow is like a small team photo of 30 big companies.
terms.example: The Dow went up when many of its 30 companies rose.
